bib.title: Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples

read.skipped: Supplementary Material (prompts, ablation, model comparison, sampling parameters, costs) is not in the PDF

question: Can a language model conditioned on real sociodemographic backstories act as a proxy for specific human subpopulations in social science research?
hypothesis: GPT-3 has high algorithmic fidelity: properly conditioned, its response distributions mirror those of fine-grained human subgroups.
contributions: conceptualizes algorithmic fidelity and identifies four criteria to assess it
introduces silicon sampling, a methodology by which a language model can generate a virtual population of respondents, correcting skewed marginal statistics in the training data
introduces a novel approach to conditioning on first-person demographic backstories to simulate targeted human survey responses
presents evidence for algorithmic fidelity in GPT-3 in the domain of U.S. politics and public opinion
provides examples of how the model can be used for social science research

method.summary: Each real survey respondent (ANES 2012/2016/2020, Pigeonholing Partisans) is turned into a first-person backstory prompt; GPT-3 completes it to produce one silicon subject per human. Silicon and human samples are compared via human raters (Study 1), tetrachoric correlation and agreement on vote choice (Study 2), and Cramer's V across survey items (Study 3). No training.
method.task: simulating survey respondents with conditioned LM completions

datasets.name: Pigeonholing Partisans (Rothschild et al. 2019)
datasets.preprocessing: regex extraction of final four words from each GPT-3 sample

datasets.name: ANES 2012, 2016, 2020
datasets.preprocessing: vote coded 1 Republican, 0 Democrat; GPT-3 probability dichotomized at 0.50

inference.decoding: probabilistic sampling; Study 2 uses next-token probabilities of Republican vs Democratic candidate for 'In [year], I voted for...'
inference.samples: one silicon subject per human participant; variation across sampling parameters reported only in Supplementary Material
inference.prompting: Study 1: first-person backstory template with demographics inserted, completion yields four words. Study 2: ANES variables (race/ethnicity, gender, age, ideology, party ID, political interest, church attendance, discusses politics, flag patriotism (not 2020), state (not 2020)) as backstory. Study 3: interview-style template, 11 ANES answers as context, predict the twelfth, options given by 'Interviewer'.

metrics.name: proportion agreement

metrics.name: Cramer's V
metrics.definition: association between each pair of survey items, computed in ANES and in GPT-3 output

baselines: human data (no model baselines in main text; alternative language models only in Supplementary Material)
eval.protocol: Study 1: 2,873 Lucid raters, eight random lists each, three raters per list, OLS with evaluator fixed effects and clustered SEs. Studies 2-3: aggregate comparison, not individual-level.

limits: Only GPT-3, only US politics and public opinion; authors invite work on other fields
Group-level distribution match only; no individual-level correspondence evaluated
No numeric thresholds for algorithmic fidelity; authors decline to set them
Pure independents poorly predicted, esp. 2020; mild marginal bias in each year
Prompts, ablation, model comparison, sampling-parameter variation and costs are in the Supplementary Material, not read
Authors flag misuse risk: targeted misinformation, manipulation, fraud
2020 result partly tests data after the 2019 corpus end but with variables like state and flag patriotism missing

terms.definition: the degree to which the complex patterns of relationships between ideas, attitudes, and sociocultural contexts within a model accurately mirror those within a range of human subpopulations
conditioning the model on backstories drawn from a known representative sample (e.g. ANES) to correct skewed marginals
